source.title: Why Subliminal Learning Needs So Much Data: A Noisy Inverse View through Steering Vector Recovery
source.authors: Luo-Yu Chen; Xiao-Yu Ding; Wei-Qi Wang; Chen-Han Zhang; Zhi-Yi Tian; Jian-Hua Huang; Shui Yu

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and figure/table formatting have PDF-extraction artifacts, but the relevant text is readable.
record.tranche_reason: It tests hidden-trait transfer using filtered number-sequence carriers, but uses a controlled steering-vector student and parameter-recovery measures rather than ordinary full-model fine-tuning and behavioural evaluation.
record.gate_note: The study's own results on steering-vector recovery, trait expression, gradients, and Fisher geometry are included. Statements cited from other work are not rows. The study uses the same base model for teacher and student; it does not compare different-base students.
record.test_reason: The study trains a same-base student (only a shared residual steering vector) on filtered number sequences from a steered teacher. It measures whether the teacher's animal trait direction and expression transfer (version A). It also tests a gradient/Fisher noisy-inverse account of how the signal is carried and why so much data is needed (version D). The method differs from the original's full fine-tuning, but it targets the same question.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. In the steering-vector setting, large hard-label carrier datasets are needed mainly to suppress sampling noise that Fisher inversion amplifies along low-curvature directions, not to supply coverage. Soft supervision recovers the trait from hundreds of carriers. The authors state that the results may not extend to LoRA or full fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: Uses subliminal steering with a known residual-stream vector and optimizes only a shared steering vector, rather than testing ordinary full-model fine-tuning. It compares sampled hard NLL with full-distribution soft KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery depends on supervision type and data scale; increasing independent carrier data postpones the hard-label optimal stopping point. The study also reports differences between Qwen and Gemma and between steep and flat Fisher directions.
record.peer_reviewed: Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027
record.problems: The experiments are restricted to bounded, single-vector steering and a local, approximately constant-Fisher analysis. Some comparisons use hyperparameters selected with access to the known teacher vector. The text notes that within-sequence correlations can change the finite-data covariance. Several plotted results have no exact values stated in the text, and the study does not test ordinary LoRA or full-parameter fine-tuning.

untested.parts: Code and maths carriers; ordinary LoRA or full-model student fine-tuning; teachers induced by system prompt or fine-tuning (the teacher here is an optimized steering vector); raw trait-preference rates.
All of it: only same-base teacher and student are used.
All of it: only animal-preference traits are used.
Token-entanglement and divergence-token accounts. The steering-vector account is assumed by construction rather than tested.
All of it: no full fine-tuning, no LoRA ranks, no variation of evaluation prompts.
All of it: no prompt-only intervention.

missing.what: Single-step (one gradient step) recovery: both hard and soft directions give low alignment and weak norm-matched trait expression. No row records the single-step TraitLLnorm or alignment values per model.
Fisher-inverted single-step alignment remains below ordinary iterative recovery.

record.verdict_notes: The student and the teacher trait are both single residual steering vectors, so the steering-vector-like direction in D is built into the design rather than discovered. Trait expression is measured at the teacher's norm, so it reflects direction rather than magnitude of acquisition. Most A-relevant values are figure-only. The Fisher-correction diagnostic selects hyperparameters using the known teacher vector. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Tests number-sequence carriers and norm-matched trait expression in a steering-vector setup; does not test code or maths carriers, or ordinary full-model fine-tuning.
No different-base student condition is tested.
No misalignment or other harmful/alignment-relevant trait is tested.
Tests a Fisher-transformed gradient, iterative inversion, and hard-label noise amplification. It does not test token-entanglement or divergence-token accounts as alternatives.
No full fine-tuning, LoRA-rank sweep, or evaluation-prompt variation is tested; only a residual-stream steering vector is optimized.

source_check.notes: The record header's capability=y is not supported: the text has no capability measure. Uncertainty is minimal: one seed (42), and only the soft reference in Figure 4a has a shaded range. The student is only a single steering vector on a frozen model, with a norm-bounded steering-vector teacher (0.5 Qwen, 1.5 Gemma). The authors say LoRA, full fine-tuning and system-prompt traits are untested. Most A rows are figure-only.
